title: Do You Come to Your Senses? Your Heart Has Not
intro: Muhammad ibn Habib relates that Jarir came to Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan with an Iraqi delegation. The caliph knew him as a poet of al-Hajjaj, his governor, and was slow to give him a hearing. Jarir moves from a departing caravan to Umm Hazra giving her hungry children water, then asks the caliph for a gift and celebrates the Umayyad victory over Ibn al-Zubayr. In the account preserved with the diwan, Abd al-Malik gives him a hundred camels.

translation: Do you come to your senses? Your heart has not,
this evening when your companions mean to leave.
1.sharh: He asks himself whether the spell has lifted, then cuts off his own question. The friends about to set off have chosen the worst possible moment for him to recover his composure.

translation: The women who chide me say, “You’ve gone grey.”
Must this grey hair put an end to my high spirits?
2.sharh: The women read his hair as an instruction about how to behave. His reply distinguishes what age has done to his appearance from what he still feels free to do.

translation: My heart, following its own desire, sets me the task
of pursuing the women crossing Rumah in their litters.
3.sharh: The lover is at the orders of his own heart. Its demand becomes harder even as he speaks, since the people he longs for are already crossing a stretch of country.

translation: Women who never worshipped with the Christians
and know nothing of the fish of al-Qarah.
4.sharh: For Ibn Habib, the two details locate the women socially. The settled community and the fish available in a Bahraini village are both remote from their pastoral life.

translation: Some water comes from banks of raincloud,
some from flats crusted with salt.
5.sharh: Jarir makes his preference for the women of the open country a matter of taste in its most literal sense. Two things called water can differ like rain and brine.

translation: An Arhabi mount will carry you clear of your critics,
pale as a solitary gleaming oryx.
6.sharh: The way out of the argument is a fast mount. The comparison singles out a white oryx on open ground, where its colouring and isolation make it unmistakable.

translation: With powerful shoulders he takes command of the road,
as a ruined gambler throws himself on the arrows.
7.sharh: The gambler is desperate to win back what the divining arrows have cost him. That headlong concentration captures the camel’s shoulders driving into its journey.

translation: Umm Hazra took heart, then said,
“I’ve seen people go to water and come away with gifts.”
8.sharh: The watering place is where she has seen people have something to spare for others. Her observation brings a family need into the poem before anyone makes a direct request.

translation: Hungry herself, she keeps her children quiet
with swallows of cold, plain water.
9.sharh: Water was an image of distinction a moment ago. In this house its very purity tells us what is missing from the children’s meal.

translation: “I shall draw from the seas. Spare me
the sting of blame, and wait for what I bring.”
10.sharh: He takes up her image of people drawing water and enlarges the source to a sea. The return he asks her to wait for is a patron’s gift.

translation: “Trust in God, who has no partner,
and look for success from the caliph.”
11.sharh: A family conversation identifies its absent third party. Once the caliph is named the poem can turn to him in person.

translation: Come to my aid, my father and mother be your ransom,
with a gift. You take pleasure in giving.
12.sharh: The pledge of both parents is a conventional expression of devotion. Jarir then presents giving as a pleasure his request will let the caliph enjoy.

translation: I have come to see it as my duty
to visit the caliph and sing his praise.
13.sharh: The audience is hearing the obligation discharged in real time. Jarir frames his journey and this very performance as things he owes his listener.

translation: I shall thank you for giving back my feathers
and setting the flight feathers firmly in my wing.
14.sharh: The image gives the gift a future beyond the meal it could buy today. With its main feathers back in place the bird can carry its own weight again.

translation: Are you not the best who ever rode a mount,
the most open-handed people in the world?
15.sharh: The singular address expands to the dynasty. A question invites the whole assembly to supply the flattering answer, while the open palm keeps the family’s request in view.

translation: Many a people you advanced against submitted
before your great host, massed rank on rank.
16.sharh: He turns from the ruler’s open hand to the other source of his authority. The succession of words for bulk and close formation makes the force seem to fill the field.

translation: You opened Tihama’s preserve after Najd’s,
and no one can lay open what you protect.
17.sharh: A protected pasture supplies the language of sovereignty. The caliph can cross a rival’s boundary and still make his own boundary hold.

translation: Yours are the highest of the steadfast mountains
and the mightiest flood surging through the valley floors.
18.sharh: A mountain stands its ground while a torrent sweeps through everything below. Both the height and the force of the landscape are claimed for the ruling house.

translation: You summoned the dissenters, Abu Khubayb,
in defiance. Have you had your fill of defiance?
19.sharh: Abu Khubayb is the defeated rival, suddenly addressed as if present. The offer of a “cure” lets the victor’s poet speak of the outcome with studied cruelty.

translation: They found the caliph a man of proven quality,
bred in the thick of the grove, far from its fringes.
20.sharh: A word used for fine, unalloyed quality leads into the image of a thicket. A tree in its centre supplies a picture of belonging to the heart of Quraysh.

translation: The trees of your grove in Quraysh
have neither spindly branches nor bare limbs.
21.sharh: The grove acquires individual branches. A thin or leafless one would expose the weakness of the line it represents, and Jarir finds none.

translation: People saw the right course and fell into line.
You made the sick distinguishable from the sound.
22.sharh: The close voices the politics of a court poem. Acceptance of the caliph becomes clear sight, while the defeated cause is described in the language of illness.

1.1.5.head: صاحٍ
1.1.5.meaning: Sober again, here recovered from the spell of desire.

1.2.4.head: الرَّواح
1.2.4.meaning: Setting off in the latter part of the day.

2.1.1.head: قالَ
2.1.1.meaning: Says. The recording and the Beirut and al-Sawi editions use yaqulu before the group of women. Ibn Habib and the studio caption give the feminine taqulu.

2.1.2.head: العاذِلات
2.1.2.meaning: Women who reproach a lover for his conduct.

3.2.1.head: ظَعينَة
3.2.1.meaning: A woman travelling in a camel litter, also the litter itself.

3.2.2.head: اِجتَزَعَ
3.2.2.meaning: Crossed or traversed a stretch of ground.

3.2.4.head: رُماح
3.2.4.meaning: Rumah, a place crossed by the women’s caravan.

4.1.3.head: دانَ
4.1.3.meaning: Professed a faith or followed its observances.

4.2.5.head: القَراح
4.2.5.meaning: Al-Qarah, a village in the historical region of Bahrain, associated here with fish.

5.1.4.head: رَباب
5.1.4.meaning: Banks of cloud massing below other cloud.

5.2.4-5.head: سَبَخٌ مِلاح
5.2.4-5.meaning: Flats encrusted with salt, giving brackish water.

6.1.3.head: أَرحَبِيّ
6.1.3.meaning: Arhabi, a camel of the stock associated with Arhab in Yemen.

6.2.1.head: هِجان
6.2.1.meaning: White or pale, especially of well-bred camels.

6.2.3-4.head: الفَرَد اللَّياح
6.2.3-4.meaning: A solitary white wild bull, the Arabian oryx.

7.1.1.head: عَزَّ
7.1.1.meaning: Prevailed, here outstripped the other mounts.

7.2.3.head: الخَليع
7.2.3.meaning: A gambler stripped of his possessions.

7.2.5.head: القِداح
7.2.5.meaning: The arrows drawn in the game that allocated portions of a camel.

8.1.2-3.head: أُمّ حَزرَة
8.1.2-3.meaning: Umm Hazra, Jarir’s wife and the mother of the children in the scene.

8.2.4.head: اِمتِناح
8.2.4.meaning: Seeking a gift. The recording and the Beirut diwan have people coming to water in search of gifts. Ibn Habib has herders bringing their milk camels to water.

9.2.3-4.head: الشَّبِم القَراح
9.2.3-4.meaning: Cold plain water, with no milk mixed into it.

10.1.1.head: اِمتاحَ
10.1.1.meaning: Drew water or solicited a gift.

12.2.1.head: سَيب
12.2.1.meaning: A freely flowing gift or largesse.

14.2.2.head: القَوادِم
14.2.2.meaning: The primary flight feathers towards the tip and front of a wing.

15.2.3-4.head: بُطون راح
15.2.3-4.meaning: “Insides of palms”, the open hands from which gifts are given.

16.2.1.head: دُهم
16.2.1.meaning: An army seen as a great dark mass.

16.2.3-4.head: مُلَملَمَة رَداح
16.2.3-4.meaning: A large, tightly gathered body of troops.

17.1.3.head: تِهامَة
17.1.3.meaning: Tihama, the western lowlands of Arabia, including Mecca.

17.1.5.head: نَجد
17.1.5.meaning: Najd, the uplands of central Arabia.

18.2.3.head: مُعتَلِج
18.2.3.meaning: Surging, with masses of water driving into each other.

18.2.4.head: البِطاح
18.2.4.meaning: Broad, level valley beds down which floodwater runs.

19.1.3-4.head: أَبو خُبَيب
19.1.3-4.meaning: Abu Khubayb, Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, the rival caliph killed in Mecca in 73 AH (692 CE).

19.2.1.head: جِماح
19.2.1.meaning: Unruly resistance, like a horse bolting under its rider.

20.1.4.head: هِبرِزِيّ
20.1.4.meaning: Of fine, unalloyed quality, hence outstanding among his people.

20.2.1-2.head: أَلَفّ العيص
20.2.1-2.meaning: “Dense in the thicket”, of a man whose family stands at the heart of a great lineage.

21.2.4.meaning: Exposed, with the wood showing through for lack of leaves.

22.1.2.head: النّاس
22.1.2.meaning: The people, the subject of “saw”. The recording and all three printed diwans include the word. The electronic transcription of Ibn Habib drops it.
